lesson.title: The Law That Was Supposed to Break Up the Trusts: The Sherman Antitrust Act
lesson.summary: Passed in 1890, the Sherman Antitrust Act was the first federal law to outlaw monopolistic business practices, but weak early enforcement and unclear legal language meant it took more than a decade, and several major Supreme Court cases, before it seriously threatened the trusts it targeted.
lesson.body:
By 1890, public anger at trusts and monopolies, built up over years of criticism of robber baron tactics and the near total dominance companies like Standard Oil held over their industries, had become a serious political force. Congress responded by passing the Sherman Antitrust Act, named for its chief sponsor, Senator John Sherman of Ohio, brother of Civil War general William Tecumseh Sherman. Signed into law in 1890, it was the first federal statute to declare illegal any contract, combination, or conspiracy that restrained trade between states, as well as any attempt to monopolize a market.

The law's language, however, was famously broad and vague. It did not clearly define terms like restraint of trade or monopolize, and Congress left it largely to the courts to work out what kinds of business behavior actually violated the act. This vagueness reflected a real political compromise: lawmakers wanted to be seen responding to public anger about trusts, but many were also reluctant to write specific rules that might too sharply limit the very business practices, including horizontal integration and vertical integration, that had built the era's industrial economy.

In its first years, the Sherman Antitrust Act was enforced weakly and often in ways that reformers had not intended. Federal prosecutors and courts frequently applied the law's restraint of trade language against labor unions rather than against corporations, since a union organizing a strike across state lines could technically be described as restraining interstate trade. The most notable example came in 1895, in the case In re Debs, when the Supreme Court upheld the use of an injunction based partly on this reasoning against Eugene Debs and the American Railway Union during the Pullman Strike. That same year, in United States versus E.C. Knight Company, the Supreme Court ruled that manufacturing was not itself interstate commerce, sharply limiting the federal government's ability to use the act against manufacturing trusts like the sugar refining monopoly at the center of that case.

Real enforcement against the trusts the law had been designed to target did not begin in earnest until the presidency of Theodore Roosevelt, who took office in 1901. Roosevelt used the Sherman Antitrust Act far more aggressively than his predecessors, most notably in the 1904 Supreme Court case Northern Securities Company versus United States, which broke up a railroad holding company controlled by financiers including J.P. Morgan, and later in the landmark 1911 case Standard Oil Company of New Jersey versus United States, which broke John D. Rockefeller's oil trust into more than thirty separate companies. These decisions, made possible only by the Supreme Court's power of judicial review to interpret and apply the act's broad language to real cases, finally demonstrated that antitrust law could seriously threaten even the largest and most powerful trusts.

The Sherman Antitrust Act remains the foundation of American antitrust law today, and its passage marked a turning point in the relationship between government and big business. After decades in which the rise of big business had proceeded with minimal government interference, the act established, at least in principle, that the federal government had both the authority and the responsibility to police competition and restrain the concentrated economic power that trusts and monopolies represented, even if it took years of legal battles to make that principle a practical reality.
